--- title: "8. Calibrating cash flows from data" aliases: [/measuring-leverage.html] --- Everything so far priced the cash-flow processes of Table II as given. This chapter is where those numbers come from — and, more importantly, where they do *not* come from. The characteristic that separates value from growth in this model is not a return beta, not an average return, not a valuation ratio. It is how hard a claim's *dividends* load on the persistent component of consumption growth. That loading is measured by a regression whose right-hand side contains only consumption. There is no return anywhere on the page. This discipline is the whole point of the exercise. [Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd) showed that a DCF can rationalize any premium because its discount rate is a free number fitted to the returns it claims to explain. Here the household was calibrated to consumption moments alone ([Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd)), and each claim brings only its cash-flow numbers. When the model later produces a value premium, that premium will be an output, because nothing in this chapter ever saw one. The plan: build the paper's proxy for expected consumption growth, run the paper's equation (19) on the dividends of the growth, value, and market claims, and see the risk sit exactly where the model needs it — in value's cash flows. Then I explain how these annual slopes relate to the monthly loadings the solver actually uses. ## The economics: one regression, no returns Expected consumption growth $x_t$ is not observable. But it is persistent, and consumption growth is expected growth plus noise: $\Delta c_{t+1} = \mu + x_t + \sigma_t \eta_{t+1}$. Averaging the last few years of realized growth averages the noise away and leaves an estimate of where $x_t$ has recently been. The paper uses a two-year moving average of *lagged* consumption growth — lagged, so the current year's dividend innovation never sits on both sides of the regression. Equation (19) of the paper regresses each claim's dividend growth on that proxy: $$ \Delta d_t \;=\; d_0 \;+\; \tilde\phi \, \tfrac{1}{2}\!\sum_{k=1}^{2} \Delta c_{t-k} \;+\; \varepsilon_t . $$ {#eq-nineteen} The slope $\tilde\phi$ is the annual, estimable counterpart of the monthly leverage parameter $\phi$ from [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd): it answers *when the slow component of consumption growth is one point higher, how much faster do this claim's dividends grow?* If the long-run risks story of the value premium is right, value's $\tilde\phi$ must come out well above growth's — measured from cash flows alone, before any return is looked at. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Derivation: why the moving average identifies the loading"} Take the dividend process of [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd), $\Delta d_{t+1} = \mu_d + \phi x_t + \varphi_\sigma \sigma_t u_{t+1}$, and the consumption process $\Delta c_{t+1} = \mu + x_t + \sigma_t \eta_{t+1}$. A window-$w$ average of lagged consumption growth is $\frac{1}{w}\sum_k \Delta c_{t-k} = \mu + \frac{1}{w}\sum_k x_{t-k-1} + \text{noise}$. Because $x_t$ is highly persistent, the average of its recent lags is close to $x_t$ itself, so the regressor is (noisy) $x_t$ plus a constant, and the population slope of $\Delta d$ on it is $\phi$ times an attenuation factor that depends on the signal-to-noise ratio of the proxy and on time aggregation. The attenuation is common across claims run against the *same* regressor, which is why the regression identifies the *ordering and relative size* of the loadings cleanly, while the level of each annual slope is not the monthly $\phi$. ::: Two clocks, one mapping. The regression above runs on annual data, because that is the frequency at which seven decades of portfolio dividends exist. The solver runs on monthly data. The annual slopes are therefore *not* the numbers Table II feeds the solver. They do two jobs: they establish the ranking the monthly loadings must respect, and they are the data panel of the paper's Table VI. The monthly Table II loadings ($\phi_G = 2.6$, $\phi_V = 6.2$, $\phi_m = 2.8$) are then chosen so that when the *model* is simulated and equation (19) is run on the simulated annual data, the model's slopes match the data's — that is Table VI's model panel. Cash flows are matched to cash flows, on both clocks; returns enter neither. ## Hands-on: measuring the loadings The reconstruction of the 1930–2003 series (consumption growth, portfolio dividend growth from the book-to-market sort) was built in [Chapter 2](02-value-premium-in-the-data.qmd); here I only load the committed CSVs. ::: {#f4349640 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this # notebook runs outside the repository. from pathlib import Path import urllib.request DATA = Path("../../data") if not DATA.exists(): DATA = Path("data") DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True) base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/" "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/") for f in ("annual_panel.csv", "consumption_annual.csv", "rf_annual.csv"): if not (DATA / f).exists(): urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f) ``` ::: ::: {#d8d03e0c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import lrrcs as lrr dc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv").sort_values("year") panel = pd.read_csv(DATA / "annual_panel.csv") y = dc["dc"].to_numpy() ``` ::: `lrr.expected_growth_proxy` builds the two-year moving average of lagged growth. The first two years have no lags to average, so they are missing by construction: ::: {#c6422fb9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ma = lrr.expected_growth_proxy(y, window=2) pd.DataFrame({"year": dc["year"], "dc": y, "ma": ma}).round(3).head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
year dc ma

4 1934 0.062 -0.055
5 1935 0.042 0.020
``` ::: ::: ::: {#18fbb1ad .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib matplotlib.use("Agg") import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2)) ax.plot(dc["year"], y, color="#1b1714", lw=1.1, label="annual Δc") ax.plot(dc["year"], ma, color="#7a1f1f", lw=1.8, label="two-year MA of lags") ax.axhline(0, color="#888888", lw=0.6) ax.set_xlabel("year") ax.set_ylabel("consumption growth") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: Now @eq-nineteen, once per claim. The value portfolio's dividend series has two missing depression years, so the regression masks non-finite observations; the cell prints the count so nothing is silently dropped. ::: {#b3e50b38 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} def dgrowth(claim): rows = panel[panel["claim"] == claim].merge(dc, on="year").sort_values("year") return rows["dgrowth"].to_numpy() def phi_tilde(dd): ok = np.isfinite(ma) & np.isfinite(dd) xx = ma[ok] - ma[ok].mean() ee = dd[ok] - dd[ok].mean() return float(xx @ ee / (xx @ xx)) print({c: round(phi_tilde(dgrowth(c)), 3) for c in ("Growth", "Value", "Market")}) print("missing value-portfolio years:", int(np.sum(~np.isfinite(dgrowth("Value"))))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {'Growth': -0.267, 'Value': 12.129, 'Market': 0.722} missing value-portfolio years: 2 ``` ::: ::: There is the risk, in the cash flows, where the model said it would be. Value's dividend growth rises hard with the slow component of consumption; growth's barely responds — on this reconstruction it even leans slightly the other way — and the market sits in between. ::: {#d8aef398 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6)) for claim, color in (("Growth", "#1b1714"), ("Value", "#7a1f1f")): dd = dgrowth(claim) ok = np.isfinite(ma) & np.isfinite(dd) ax.scatter(ma[ok], dd[ok], s=16, color=color, label=claim.lower(), alpha=0.8) slope = phi_tilde(dd) grid_x = np.linspace(ma[ok].min(), ma[ok].max(), 2) ax.plot(grid_x, dd[ok].mean() + slope * (grid_x - ma[ok].mean()), color=color, lw=1.4) ax.set_xlabel("two-year MA of lagged Δc") ax.set_ylabel("dividend growth Δd") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: How do these numbers compare with the paper? My Table VI reports $-0.38$ for growth, $2.16$ for value, and $0.66$ for the market; the reconstruction prints $-0.267$, $12.129$, and $0.722$. The market slope lands close, the growth slope is small and negative in both, and value is far above growth in both — but the value *point estimate* is wildly different. That is what seventy-odd annual observations buy: a claim's slope moves a lot with the data vintage and with the two masked depression years, which fall exactly where consumption swings were largest. The deliverable of this regression is the ordering — value loads hard on long-run consumption news, growth does not — and the ordering is what survives. Do not read a third decimal, or even a first one, into the value slope. The package wraps the same arithmetic. `lrr.estimate_long_run_leverage` is the one-claim slope, and `lrr.calibrate_from_data` turns consumption and dividend-growth series into a full set of cash-flow parameters. Look at the signatures: there is no argument that accepts a return. The function will not take one. That is the structural discipline of the calibration, enforced by the API itself. ::: {#3acef880 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(round(lrr.estimate_long_run_leverage(y, dgrowth("Market"), window=2), 3)) lrr.print_calibration_summary( lrr.calibrate_from_data(y, market=dgrowth("Market"), frequency="annual", window=2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.722 Portfolio μ (m) φ (long-run) φ_σ α ------------------------------------------------------- market 0.00076 0.722 5.33 0.57 ``` ::: ::: Same 0.722 as the manual regression, plus the volatility loading $\varphi_\sigma$ and the short-run correlation $\alpha$ estimated from the residuals of the same regression — still no returns. Finally, the mapping to the solver's clock. Table II's monthly loadings are the numbers everything downstream prices: ::: {#510817b7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} params = lrr.get_table_ii_params() for name, d in params.dividends.items(): print(f"{name:8s} monthly phi = {d.phi}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` growth monthly phi = 2.6 value monthly phi = 6.2 market monthly phi = 2.8 ``` ::: ::: The monthly $\phi$ are larger than the annual slopes because time aggregation and the noisy proxy attenuate the annual regression (see the derivation callout above). What disciplines them is Table VI's model panel: simulate the economy at these monthly loadings, aggregate to years, rerun @eq-nineteen, and the simulated slopes have to look like the data's. The ordering — $\phi_V = 6.2$ far above $\phi_G = 2.6$, market at $2.8$ — is the annual regression's ordering, carried to the monthly clock. ## Takeaways - The characteristic is cash-flow leverage: the slope of dividend growth on a two-year moving average of lagged consumption growth (paper eq. 19). Returns appear nowhere in the calibration, and `calibrate_from_data` has no argument that could accept one. - On the reconstruction the slopes print $-0.267$ (growth), $12.129$ (value), $0.722$ (market); my Table VI reports $-0.38$, $2.16$, $0.66$. The point estimates are noisy — the ordering, value far above growth with the market in between, is the robust deliverable. - The annual slopes are not the solver's inputs. Table II's monthly loadings ($2.6$, $6.2$, $2.8$) are chosen so the model's simulated eq.-19 slopes match the data's; the annual regression fixes the ordering and provides the check. ## Exercises 1. Rerun the three regressions with `lrr.expected_growth_proxy(y, window=3)`. Does the ordering of the slopes survive a different window? 2. Drop the years 1930–1945 from the sample and re-estimate. Does value still carry the larger $\tilde\phi$? What happens to the growth slope's sign? 3. Call `lrr.calibrate_from_data(y, market=dgrowth("Market"))` and then try to pass the market's *returns* to it in any argument. Confirm from the error that there is no place for them. ::: {.firewall} **Where each number comes from.** Every number above is printed by the cells on this page: the slopes by the eq.-19 OLS and `estimate_long_run_leverage` / `calibrate_from_data` on `data/consumption_annual.csv` and `data/annual_panel.csv`, the monthly loadings by `get_table_ii_params`; Table VI's $-0.38$ / $2.16$ / $0.66$ are the paper's prints. Download the chapter as a notebook (top of the page) to rerun everything. :::
